claims.text: A temperature-dependent interatomic-potential framework can be applied to bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed potential explicitly incorporates scattering from defects such as 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed potential explicitly incorporates anharmonic lattice effects.
Explicit treatment of defects and anharmonicity will produce significantly more accurate conductivity predictions than traditional perfect-crystal models.
Quantum and defect-scattering effects dominate conductivity from nearly 0 to 200 K.
Anharmonic vibrational behavior becomes crucial for conductivity from 300 to 1200 K.
Defects mediate scattering through lattice distortions.
Oxygen impurities induce local electronic effects that modify conductivity.
The potential captures defect-induced modifications to conductivity.
The potential captures anharmonic vibrational modifications to conductivity.
Both electronic and phononic transport channels contribute to the modeled conductivity.
Explicitly modeling defect and anharmonic scattering adjusts electronic and phononic transport channels as functions of temperature.
Conventional analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals and neglect important scattering and anharmonic effects.
These conventional assumptions cause systematic deviations from experimental conductivity measurements for HfNbTaTiZr.
For the 1 wt.% oxygen sample, the framework will capture the additional scattering and match measurements more closely than conventional models.
The framework is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr only within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Application outside the specified temperatures or to substantially different defect types or concentrations requires recalibration.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement depends on parameterization of defect-scattering rates and anharmonic contributions.

contradictions.description: The target quantity is not consistently defined. The mechanism invokes both electronic and phononic contributions, which describes thermal conductivity, and the cited conductivity evidence is thermal; however, the falsification experiment specifies electrical-conductivity measurements only. Electrical conductivity alone cannot benchmark the claimed phonon contribution.
